title: The Wizard of Oz
author: L. Frank Baum
ru: Смерч уносит девочку Дороти в волшебную страну Оз, и она с новыми друзьями идёт к Волшебнику, чтобы вернуться домой.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Cyclone
chapters.text:
Dorothy lived in the middle of the great Kansas prairies — flat land with no trees, only grass, for miles and miles. She lived with Uncle Henry, who was a farmer, and Aunt Em, his wife. Their house had only one room. Under the floor there was a small dark hole called a cyclone cellar. A cyclone is a terrible wind that turns round and round, and it can break a house like a matchbox. When a cyclone came, the family hid in the cellar.

Everything in Kansas was grey. The sun burned the grass grey. The rain washed the house grey. Even Uncle Henry and Aunt Em were grey and tired, and they never laughed. When Dorothy first came to live with them, her laugh frightened Aunt Em so much that she put her hand on her heart.

But Dorothy had Toto. Toto was a little black dog with long silky hair and small black eyes that shone with fun. He played all day long, and Dorothy loved him dearly.

One afternoon the sky was even greyer than usual. Uncle Henry stood at the door and looked at it. From the north came a long, low cry of the wind.

“There's a cyclone coming, Em,” he said. “I'll go and look after the animals.” And he ran to the cowshed.

Aunt Em dropped her work. “Quick, Dorothy!” she screamed. “Run for the cellar!”

She opened the little door in the floor and climbed down the ladder into the dark. Dorothy picked up Toto, but he jumped out of her arms and hid under the bed. Dorothy ran after him. She was halfway across the room when the house shook so hard that she fell down on the floor.

Then a strange thing happened. The house turned round two or three times and rose slowly into the air, like a balloon.

It was in the very centre of the cyclone now. The wind carried it up and away, mile after mile, as easily as you carry a feather.

Inside, it was very dark, and the wind howled all around. Toto ran round the room, barking. Suddenly he fell through the open door in the floor! Dorothy thought he was lost. Then she saw one of his ears in the hole. The strong wind was holding him up! She caught Toto by the ear, pulled him back into the room, and shut the door.

Hours passed. Nothing bad happened, and slowly Dorothy began to feel calmer.

“Perhaps the house will fall and break into pieces,” she thought. “But I can't do anything about it, so why worry?”

She climbed onto her bed and lay down with Toto in her arms. The house was rocking gently, like a baby's cradle, and soon she was fast asleep.

A sudden, hard bump woke her up. The house was not moving any more. Bright sunshine was coming in through the window.

Dorothy jumped up, ran to the door, and opened it. What she saw made her cry out in surprise.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Silver Shoes
chapters.text:
The house stood in a beautiful green country, full of fruit trees, bright flowers and singing birds. After the grey prairies, it looked like a dream.

Then some very strange people came towards Dorothy. They were no taller than Dorothy, but they looked much older. The three men wore blue clothes and tall pointed hats with little bells, and the woman wore a white dress covered in tiny stars.

The old woman bowed low. “Welcome to the land of the Munchkins,” she said. “Thank you for killing the Wicked Witch of the East! Now our people are free.”

“You're very kind,” said Dorothy, “but there must be a mistake. I didn't kill anybody.”

“Your house did,” said the old woman, “and that is the same thing. Look!” She pointed to the corner of the house. Two feet in silver shoes were sticking out from under it.

“Oh dear!” cried Dorothy. “What can we do?”

“Nothing,” said the old woman calmly. “She was very wicked. She made the Munchkins work for her like slaves. I am the Witch of the North.”

“A real witch?” Dorothy took a step back.

“Yes, but a good one. There were four witches in the Land of Oz. The Witches of the North and the South are good. The Witch of the East was wicked — and so is the Witch of the West.”

Just then the Munchkins gave a shout. The dead Witch's feet were gone! Only the silver shoes were left.

“She was so old that she dried up in the sun,” said the Witch of the North. She shook the dust out of the shoes and gave them to Dorothy. “They're yours now.”

“There is some magic in them,” said one of the Munchkins, “but we never found out what it is.”

“Thank you,” said Dorothy. “But I must go home to my aunt and uncle in Kansas. Can you show me the way?”

The Munchkins shook their heads. All around the Land of Oz, they said, there was a great desert, and nobody could cross it alive. Dorothy began to cry. At once the kind little Munchkins took out their handkerchiefs and cried too.

The Witch took off her hat and balanced it on the end of her nose. “One, two, three,” she counted in a serious voice. At once the hat became a little board with big white letters: LET DOROTHY GO TO THE CITY OF EMERALDS.

“Is your name Dorothy, my dear?” she asked.

“Yes,” said Dorothy, drying her eyes.

“Then you must go to the Emerald City — the city of green jewels — and ask the Great Wizard Oz for help. He is more powerful than all of us witches. Just follow the yellow brick road.”

“Will you come with me?” asked Dorothy.

“I can't. But I'll give you my kiss. Nobody will dare to hurt a girl with the kiss of the Witch of the North.”

She kissed Dorothy gently on the forehead, and her lips left a round, shining mark there. Then she turned round three times on her left heel — and disappeared.

Dorothy put on the silver shoes. They fitted her perfectly, as if they were made for her.

She didn't know it yet, but those shoes had a great secret.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. A Man of Straw and a Man of Tin
chapters.text:
Dorothy and Toto set off along the yellow brick road. It ran past neat blue Munchkin houses and green fields.

At midday Dorothy stopped to rest by a cornfield. In the middle of the field stood a scarecrow on a tall pole — a man of old clothes and straw, made to frighten the birds away. His head was a small sack with a painted face and an old blue hat on top.

As Dorothy was looking at the painted face, one of its eyes slowly winked at her.

Then the Scarecrow nodded at her in a friendly way.

“Good day,” he said in a rather dry voice.

“Did you speak?” asked Dorothy in wonder.

“Certainly. How do you do?”

“Very well, thank you,” said Dorothy politely. “And you?”

“Not very well. It's terribly boring up here, scaring crows day and night. Could you help me down?”

Dorothy lifted him off the pole. He was as light as a pillow.

“Thank you very much. I feel like a new man! Where are you going?”

“To the Emerald City, to ask the great Oz to send me home to Kansas.”

“Do you think,” said the Scarecrow slowly, “that Oz could give me some brains? My head is full of straw, you see. I haven't got any brains at all.”

“I don't know,” said Dorothy. “But you can come with me and ask him.”

“Oh, thank you! My body is only straw, but I don't mind, because I can't feel pain. If somebody steps on my toe, it doesn't matter. But I don't want people to call me a fool.”

So now there were three of them. The Scarecrow often stepped into holes and fell flat on his face, but he always laughed.

That night they slept in a dark forest. In the morning they heard a deep groan nearby and found a woodman made completely of tin. He stood with his axe raised high, as still as a statue.

“Did you groan?” asked Dorothy.

“Yes,” said the Tin Woodman. “Please help me. There's an oil can in my cottage. Oil my joints!”

Dorothy ran for the oil can. She oiled his neck, then his arms, then his legs. Slowly he lowered his axe and gave a long, happy sigh.

“You saved my life,” he said. “A year ago I was chopping wood here when it began to rain. I rusted — I went stiff and red-brown, like an old nail — and I stood here like that until you came.”

When Dorothy told him about Oz, the Tin Woodman thought for a moment.

“I was once a real man,” he said, “and I loved a Munchkin girl. But the Wicked Witch of the East put a spell on my axe, and it cut me to pieces, bit by bit. A tinsmith made me a new body out of tin. But he forgot one thing — a heart. Without a heart I cannot love her. Do you think Oz could give me one?”

“Come with us and ask him,” said Dorothy.

“I'll ask for brains,” said the Scarecrow. “A fool with a heart doesn't know what to do with it.”

“I'll ask for a heart,” said the Tin Woodman. “Brains do not make anyone happy.”

They were still arguing about it when a terrible roar came from the forest.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. The Cowardly Lion
chapters.text:
The next moment a great Lion jumped onto the road. With one blow of his paw he sent the Scarecrow flying. Then he knocked down the Tin Woodman, but his sharp claws only scratched the tin.

Little Toto ran at the Lion, barking, and the great beast opened his mouth to bite him.

Dorothy didn't stop to think. She ran forward and slapped the Lion on the nose as hard as she could.

“Don't you dare bite Toto!” she cried. “You ought to be ashamed of yourself — a big beast like you, biting a poor little dog!”

“I didn't bite him,” said the Lion, rubbing his nose with his paw.

“No, but you tried to. You're nothing but a big coward.”

“I know it,” said the Lion, and he hung his head. “Everyone thinks the lion is the King of Beasts. So I roar very loudly, and everybody runs away. But if the elephants and tigers ever fought me, I would run away myself.”

A tear rolled down his nose. He wiped it away with the end of his tail.

“Perhaps Oz could give you some courage,” said Dorothy kindly.

The Lion's eyes lit up. “Then may I come with you? My life is terrible without a bit of courage.”

“Of course,” said Dorothy. “You can keep the other wild beasts away. They must be even bigger cowards than you, if you can frighten them.”

Later that day the Tin Woodman stepped on a small beetle by accident and killed it. He was so sad that he began to cry. His tears ran down onto his jaw, and it rusted shut. He couldn't say a word until Dorothy oiled it.

“From now on I'll look where I step,” he said. “If I kill another beetle, I'll cry again, and then I'll rust again.”

The next day the forest grew darker, and the Lion whispered that this was the home of the Kalidahs — wild beasts with the bodies of bears and the heads of tigers. Soon they came to a deep ditch — a long, wide crack in the ground — with no bridge across it.

The Scarecrow thought hard. “If the Tin Woodman cuts down this tall tree,” he said at last, “it will fall across the ditch, and we can walk over it.”

“That's a brilliant idea,” said the Lion. “Anyone would think you had brains in your head, not straw.”

The Woodman began to chop, and soon the tree fell with a crash across the ditch. They were just starting to cross when they heard a horrible growl. Two great Kalidahs were running towards them!

The Lion turned and roared so loudly that the beasts stopped for a second. That second was enough. Dorothy ran across with Toto in her arms, and the others followed her. But the Kalidahs jumped onto the tree and came after them.

“Quick, cut the tree!” cried the Scarecrow.

The Tin Woodman swung his axe. The tree broke — and fell, with the two growling Kalidahs, to the bottom of the ditch.

“Well,” said the Lion with a long breath, “it seems we're going to live a little longer. My heart is still beating very fast.”

“I wish I had a heart to beat,” said the Tin Woodman sadly.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. The Emerald City
chapters.text:
Soon the forest ended at a wide river. The Tin Woodman made a raft — a flat boat of tree trunks tied together — and they set off across the water.

In the middle of the river the water ran very fast. The Scarecrow, who was pushing the raft with a long pole, stuck it deep in the mud at the bottom — and couldn't pull it out again. He held on to the pole, and the raft moved on without him!

“Goodbye!” he called sadly from his pole.

At last the Lion jumped into the water and pulled the raft to the bank.

Then a kind stork carried the Scarecrow back to his friends in her long beak.

Next they came to a great field of red poppies. Their smell was dangerous: if you breathe it for a long time, you fall asleep and never wake up. Soon Dorothy's eyes began to close, and she lay down among the flowers with Toto.

“Run, Lion!” cried the Scarecrow. “You're too heavy for us to carry!”

The Lion ran off as fast as he could. The Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman did not breathe, so the poppies couldn't hurt them. They carried Dorothy and Toto out to the green grass. But the poppies were too strong for him. They found the great Lion fast asleep among the flowers, only a short way from safety.

Just then a wildcat ran past, chasing a little field mouse. The Tin Woodman lifted his axe and killed the wildcat. The mouse turned out to be the Queen of the Field Mice!

“How can I thank you?” she asked.

“Can you help us save our friend the Lion?” said the Scarecrow.

The Queen called, and thousands of mice came running. The Tin Woodman made a little wooden cart, the mice pulled it with strings, and slowly, slowly, they took the Lion out of the field. When he woke up, he couldn't believe it.

“Saved by mice!” he said. “What a strange world this is.”

At last they saw a beautiful green light in the sky. It was the Emerald City! At its great gate, covered in emeralds, they met a little man dressed all in green — the Guardian of the Gates.

“You want to see Oz?” he said in surprise. “He is powerful and terrible. If you come for a silly reason, he may destroy you all in a moment.” Then he put a pair of green glasses on each of them and locked them with a little gold key. “The city is so bright that it would blind you,” he explained.

Inside, everything was green — the streets, the houses, the people, even the sunshine. The next day the friends were taken to the Throne Room, one by one.

Dorothy saw an enormous Head with no body, floating above a green throne.

“I am Oz, the Great and Terrible,” said the Head. “Who are you, and why do you seek me?”

The Scarecrow saw a lovely lady with wings. The Tin Woodman saw a terrible beast with five eyes and five arms. The Lion saw a ball of fire so hot that he ran back to the door.

But each of them heard the same answer:

“I never give anything for nothing. Kill the Wicked Witch of the West. Then — and only then — I will give you what you want.”

chapters.title: Chapter 6. The Wicked Witch of the West
chapters.text:
“But I can't kill anybody!” Dorothy cried to her friends. “And even if I wanted to, how could I kill a witch?”

Nobody wanted to kill anyone. But they all wanted their wishes to come true, so the next morning they set off towards the setting sun.

The Wicked Witch of the West had only one eye, but it was as powerful as a telescope. From her castle door she could see her whole country. Soon she saw the strangers, and she was very angry.

She blew on a silver whistle, and forty great wolves came running.

“Go and tear those strangers to pieces,” she ordered.

But the Tin Woodman was ready with his axe. Soon all forty wolves lay dead in front of him.

The Witch was furious. She blew her whistle twice, and forty wild crows flew to her. “Fly to the strangers,” she screamed, “and peck out their eyes!”

But the Scarecrow stood up and stretched out his arms. When the crows saw him, they were afraid, because a scarecrow's job is to frighten birds. The Scarecrow caught each crow that came near and twisted its neck.

Next the Witch sent a black cloud of angry bees. The Scarecrow quickly took the straw out of his body and covered Dorothy, Toto and the Lion with it. So the bees flew at the Tin Woodman, broke all their stings on his hard tin body, and died. Then Dorothy helped to put the straw back into the Scarecrow.

Then the Witch sent her soldiers, the Winkies — little men dressed in yellow, with sharp spears. But the Lion gave a great roar, and they ran back to the castle as fast as they could.

Now the Witch had only one thing left: the Golden Cap. The owner of this Cap could call the Winged Monkeys three times, and they had to obey. The Witch put on the Cap, stood on one foot, and said the magic words:

“Ep-pe, pep-pe, kak-ke! Hil-lo, hol-lo, hel-lo! Ziz-zy, zuz-zy, zik!”

The sky went dark, and a great crowd of monkeys with huge wings came flying through the air.

“Destroy the strangers,” said the Witch. “All except the Lion. Bring him to me — I'll make him work like a horse.”

Some of the Monkeys carried the Tin Woodman high over a valley full of sharp rocks and dropped him. He landed with a crash and lay there, bent and broken. Others pulled all the straw out of the Scarecrow and threw his clothes into a tall tree. Then they tied up the Lion and carried him to the castle.

Last of all, the King of the Monkeys flew down to Dorothy. His long, hairy arms reached out — and stopped. He saw the shining mark of the good Witch's kiss on her forehead.

“We cannot harm this girl,” he said. “She is protected by the Power of Good, and that is stronger than the Power of Evil.”

So they carried her gently to the castle instead.

The Witch saw the mark on Dorothy's forehead and was frightened. Then she saw the silver shoes and began to shake, because she knew how powerful they were. But when she looked into Dorothy's innocent eyes, she understood: the girl did not know about the magic in her own shoes.

The Witch smiled an evil smile. “I can still make her my slave,” she thought.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. A Bucket of Water
chapters.text:
Dorothy had to work all day in the Witch's kitchen, washing pots and sweeping floors. The Lion was locked in the yard. Every time the Witch came near him, he roared, so she gave him no food. But at night Dorothy secretly brought him something to eat.

The Witch wanted the silver shoes more than anything, but Dorothy took them off only at night and for her bath. The Witch was afraid of the dark, so she never came into Dorothy's room at night. And she was even more afraid of water — she never touched it at all.

So the Witch thought of a trick. She put an iron bar in the middle of the kitchen floor and used magic to make it invisible, so nobody could see it. When Dorothy walked across the room, she fell over it, and one of her silver shoes came off. The Witch grabbed it at once and put it on her own thin foot.

“Give me back my shoe!” cried Dorothy.

“I won't,” laughed the Witch. “It's my shoe now. And one day I'll get the other one too!”

This made Dorothy so angry that she picked up a bucket of water and threw it all over the Witch.

The Witch screamed. Then, as Dorothy watched in amazement, she began to get smaller and smaller.

“See what you've done!” she cried. “In a minute I'll melt away!”

“I'm very sorry,” said Dorothy, who was really frightened. “I didn't know.”

“Didn't you know that water would be the end of me?” screamed the Witch. “Well — I'm going now!”

With these words she melted into a brown, shapeless mess on the clean kitchen floor. Dorothy picked up the silver shoe, put it back on, and ran out to the yard.

“Lion!” she cried. “The Wicked Witch is dead! We're free!”

The Winkies were free too. They brought the poor Tin Woodman back from the rocks, and the Winkie tinsmiths worked for three days to hammer his bent body straight again. Then they found the Scarecrow's clothes in the tall tree and filled them with fresh straw. Soon both friends were as good as new.

Dorothy found the Golden Cap in the Witch's cupboard. The magic words were written inside it, so she called the Winged Monkeys, and they carried the friends all the way back to the Emerald City.

But the great Oz kept them waiting for days. At last the Scarecrow sent him a message: “See us now, or we'll call the Winged Monkeys!” Oz was afraid of the Monkeys, so he agreed.

The next morning they went into the Throne Room. It was empty.

“Where are you?” asked Dorothy.

“I am everywhere,” said a deep Voice. “Come back tomorrow. I need time to think.”

“No!” cried Dorothy. “You must keep your promise!”

The Lion gave a terrible roar. Toto jumped away in fright and knocked over a screen in the corner. Behind it stood a little old man with a bald head and a wrinkled face. He looked just as surprised as they were.

“Who are you?” shouted the Tin Woodman, raising his axe.

“I am Oz, the Great and Terrible,” said the little man in a shaking voice. “Please don't hit me! I'll do anything you want.”

“Aren't you a great Wizard?” asked Dorothy.

The little man looked down at the floor. “No, my dear. I'm just a common man. I'm a humbug — a cheat.”

chapters.title: Chapter 8. There Is No Place Like Home
chapters.text:
The little man told them his story. He came from Omaha, in America, where he flew a balloon at a circus. One day the wind carried his balloon away to the Land of Oz. The people saw him come down from the clouds and thought he was a great wizard. He let them believe it. “And the Emerald City isn't really green,” he added. “It's the glasses!”

“I'm a very good man,” he said, “but I'm a very bad Wizard.”

Still, he kept his promise. He filled the Scarecrow's head with bran mixed with pins and needles. “Now your brains are sharp,” he said, and the Scarecrow felt very wise indeed. He put a red silk heart into the Tin Woodman's chest. And he gave the Lion a green drink. “Drink it, and courage will be inside you.” The Lion drank every drop and felt braver at once.

For Dorothy he made a new balloon of green silk. “We'll fly back to America together,” he said.

Oz climbed into the basket. But at the last minute, Toto ran after a kitten, and Dorothy ran after Toto. When she caught him, the balloon was already rising into the sky.

“Come back!” she screamed. “I want to go too!”

“I can't come back, my dear!” called Oz. “Goodbye!”

And that was the last that anyone ever saw of Oz, the Wonderful Wizard.

Dorothy cried bitterly, until a soldier told her about Glinda, the Good Witch of the South. Perhaps Glinda could help?

So the friends set off for the South. On the way, the Lion killed a giant spider that was eating the animals of a forest, and the grateful animals made him their king. At last Dorothy stood before Glinda and told her everything.

“Your silver shoes can carry you over the desert,” said Glinda. “Just knock your heels together three times and tell them where you want to go. They could take you home even on your first day in Oz. You just didn't know it.”

“But then I wouldn't have my wonderful brains!” cried the Scarecrow.

“And I wouldn't have my lovely heart,” said the Tin Woodman.

“And I would be a coward for ever,” said the Lion.

Dorothy gave Glinda the Golden Cap. “The Winged Monkeys will carry your friends to their new homes,” said Glinda. “The Scarecrow will rule the Emerald City, the Tin Woodman will rule the Winkies, and the Lion will go back to his forest. Then I'll set the Monkeys free.”

Dorothy hugged her friends goodbye. The Tin Woodman cried so much that Dorothy had to oil his jaw one last time. Then she took Toto in her arms, knocked her heels together three times and said:

“Take me home to Aunt Em!”

She flew so fast that the wind whistled in her ears — and then she was rolling on the grass.

She sat up. She was on the wide Kansas prairie, in front of Uncle Henry's new farmhouse, and he was milking the cows. The silver shoes were gone — lost somewhere over the desert for ever.

Aunt Em ran out of the house, crying and laughing at once.

“My darling child!” she cried, covering Dorothy's face with kisses. “Where in the world did you come from?”

“From the Land of Oz,” said Dorothy seriously. “And here is Toto too. Oh, Aunt Em, I'm so glad to be at home again! There is no place like home.”
